stem: Spending five silent childhood years memorizing Shakespeare and Dunbar before finding her booming voice, who authored I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings?
ahaFactoid: To write uninterrupted, Angelou rented bare local hotel rooms at dawn—stripping wall art and keeping only a Bible, sherry, and legal pads!

stem: Punctuating every death—from bombed soldiers to flat champagne—with the dry refrain "So it goes" 106 times in Slaughterhouse-Five, which satirist survived Dresden as a POW?
ahaFactoid: Before fame hit, Vonnegut ran an early Cape Cod Saab dealership—joking Swedes denied him a Nobel Prize because he was so bad at selling cars!

stem: Sci-Fi Wire, 1942: Tired of pulp stories where metal servants always ran amok, prolific biochemist [ _____ ] coined "robotics" and drafted the Three Laws.
ahaFactoid: Asimov wrote or edited over 500 books spanning nine of the ten main Dewey Decimal categories—missing only Philosophy!

stem: A tattered X-marked parchment of Spyglass Hill, a crutch tucked under one arm, and a green parrot shrieking "Pieces of eight!": who charms young Jim Hawkins on the Hispaniola?
ahaFactoid: Robert Louis Stevenson based Silver's booming charisma and missing leg on his real poet friend William Ernest Henley—writer of "Invictus"!

stem: Winning the 2025 Pulitzer Prize for "James"—retelling Huckleberry Finn through Jim's razor-sharp intellect—which author also inspired the Oscar hit American Fiction?

stem: Sweeping both the Hugo and Nebula Awards in 1970, who sent envoy Genly Ai across the frozen planet Gethen in The Left Hand of Darkness?
ahaFactoid: Daughter of two famed Berkeley anthropologists, Le Guin crafted alien worlds like real field studies—complete with kinship rules and folklore!

stem: Fired as a California oil executive at age 44 during the Depression, who turned to pulp crime mags and created wisecracking L.A. sleuth Philip Marlowe?
ahaFactoid: Whenever stuck on a crime plot, Chandler famously advised pulp writers to "have a man come through a door with a gun in his hand"!

stem: Paperback Wire, 1962: Narrated by towering Chief Bromden inside an Oregon hospital ward, night orderly Ken Kesey shook counterculture readers with [ _____ ].

ahaFactoid: Stuck on stiff prose, Murakami typed his opening pages in simple English first—then translated them back to Japanese to unlock his breezy voice!

ahaFactoid: Because short dialogue lines paid the same as dense paragraphs, Dumas filled serial chapters with laconic servants giving snappy one-word replies!

stem: Stepping right past a misty drawing-room mantelpiece mirror onto a sunlit chessboard dotted with Jabberwocks, Tweedledee, and racing Red Queens: name this 1871 sequel!

stem: Sparking the biggest flood of angry subscription cancellations in New Yorker history in June 1948, which chilling Shirley Jackson story centers on a battered black box?

Homer drafted the Odyssey on paper

stem: Hailed by Plato as the "Tenth Muse," which ancient Greek lyric poet survives mostly in tantalizing torn papyrus fragments rescued from Egyptian mummy wrappings?
ahaFactoid: Out of nine ancient scrolls celebrated across Greece, only her "Ode to Aphrodite" survives intact—yet scholars still unearth lost verses today!

stem: Endless hexagonal rooms shelved with 410-page books holding every random combo of 25 symbols—hiding both gibberish and your true future: name Borges's 1941 story!

Dante penned Inferno in pure Latin

stem: Blending Roman architecture with Renaissance anatomy, Leonardo da Vinci drew a figure with outstretched arms fitting inside both a circle and a square in what ink study?
ahaFactoid: To guard its fragile 1490 ink from light damage, Venice's Accademia locks the drawing in darkness and displays it roughly once a decade!

ahaFactoid: When a client complained his leaky roof dripped straight onto his dinner table, Wright famously replied: "Well, why don't you just move the table?"

stem: When his 1877 nude sculpture The Age of Bronze looked startlingly lifelike, furious Parisian judges accused which master sculptor of secretly casting a real human body?
ahaFactoid: Rodin brought photos of his Belgian soldier model to clear his name—and deliberately sculpted later statues larger than life to stop copycat claims!

stem: A woman in a faded pink dress rests in golden Maine meadow grass, bracing thin arms as she gazes uphill toward a weathered gray clapboard farmhouse: name this 1948 icon!
ahaFactoid: Andrew Wyeth painted neighbor Anna Christina Olson, who had a nerve disorder yet fiercely refused a wheelchair—preferring to crawl across her fields!

stem: Gallery Klaxon! Three of these art-history gems hang straight on the museum wall, while one sweeping claim about a Cubist icon's skills misses completely. Spot the myth!

stem: Shimmering with genuine 24-karat gold leaf, swirling rectangles, and tiny floral circles, which radiant 1908 Viennese masterpiece by Gustav Klimt shows a kneeling embrace?
ahaFactoid: Son of a gold engraver, Klimt layered real gold and silver leaf onto his canvas—and the Austrian state bought it before it was even finished!

stem: Mid-Century Wire: Shooting brass rods outward from a gleaming central orb into a starburst of bare glowing bulbs, the atomic-age [ _____ ] defined 1960s mod living rooms.

stem: Painting 322 Saturday Evening Post covers plus the 1943 Four Freedoms series that raised $132 million in war bonds, who captured small-town America with playful humor?

stem: A black bowler hat, red tie, and buttoned dark coat against a cloudy sea—yet a floating crisp green apple hides the man's entire face: who painted The Son of Man?
ahaFactoid: Unlike wilder surrealists, Magritte lived like a quiet Brussels clerk—painting mind-benders in his tidy dining room wearing a crisp jacket and tie!

stem: Creating Montreal's gleaming 20-story Expo 67 Biosphere dome and the three-wheeled Dymaxion car, which visionary architect popularized the triangular geodesic sphere?
ahaFactoid: Chemists were so inspired by his sturdy pentagon-and-hexagon domes they named the 60-atom soccer-ball carbon molecule "buckminsterfullerene"!

stem: Amsterdam Ledger: Leaving over eighty unflinching mirrors of himself from rosy twenty-something grin to sagging bankrupt elder, Dutch master [ _____ ] invented visual memoir.
ahaFactoid: Unlike flatterers who idealized patrons, Rembrandt practiced wild scowls and raised brows in a mirror—using his own face as a free acting studio!

stem: Asking his artist wife Josephine to pose for nearly every solitary woman in his sunlit hotel rooms and late-night diners, who turned quiet urban loneliness into iconic art?
ahaFactoid: Jo kept meticulous ledgers sketching every canvas Edward finished, logging his paints, sizes, buyers, and cheeky nicknames for his characters!

stem: Rows of 8,000 life-sized clay archers, charioteers, and armored horses—each bearing unique ears, beards, and topknots—guard an underground tomb in Xi'an as what wonder?
ahaFactoid: Farmers digging a well uncovered the clay heads in 1974—the soldiers were once painted bright purple, pink, and turquoise before air faded them!

stem: Bolting a wooden shooting deck atop his station wagon to haul a 50-pound camera across Yosemite and New Mexico, who shot crisp monochrome Moonrise over Hernandez?
ahaFactoid: Trained as a concert pianist first, Adams famously compared a camera negative to a musical score—and darkroom printing to performing it live!

stem: Blueprint Klaxon! Three of these world-landmark construction facts hold up cleanly, while one dazzling Agra material claim glitters a bit too hard. Spot the myth!

Big Ben names the bell, not the tower

stem: Skipping breezy outdoor picnics for smoky gaslit rehearsal halls, which French Impressionist drew over 1,500 pastels and canvases of ballet dancers stretching?

stem: So forgotten after his 1510 death that his works gathered dust in Florence storerooms for three centuries, which Renaissance master painted Venus riding a shell?

stem: A sleek white molded fiberglass shell tapering smoothly down into one slender round aluminum stem—later gracing Star Trek's Enterprise bridge: name this 1956 seat!
ahaFactoid: Eero Saarinen swore to wipe out the "ugly, confusing slum of legs" crowding under tables—replacing four legs with one sculptural flower stem!

stem: Hauling 6,650 tons of black basalt boulders into Utah's rosy-pink Great Salt Lake in 1970, land artist Robert Smithson coiled a 1,500-foot stone curl titled what?
ahaFactoid: Salt-loving microbes tint the water bubble-gum pink, and high lake levels submerged the artwork for nearly thirty years before drought revealed it!

stem: Meaning "pictures of the floating world," which Edo-period Japanese woodblock genre shipped overseas as porcelain packing paper and electrified Monet and Van Gogh?
ahaFactoid: Van Gogh adored these bold flat-color prints so deeply he collected over 400 sheets and copied Hiroshige's rainy bridges stroke-for-stroke in oil!

stem: Turning back twenty miles on a rainy 1936 California highway, Dorothea Lange snapped seven frames inside a Nipomo pea-pickers' tent—capturing what haunting portrait?
ahaFactoid: Within days of newspapers printing Florence Owens Thompson's worried gaze, federal officials rushed 20,000 pounds of food straight to the starving camp!

stem: Louvre Wire: Crowning the grand Daru staircase as sea wind whips wet carved Parian marble drapery backward, the headless [ _____ ] once rode an ancient Greek warship prow.
ahaFactoid: Diplomat Charles Champoiseau dug up 100+ marble shards on Samothrace in 1863—and its right wing is actually a mirror-image plaster cast of the left!

stem: Straddling museum plazas on thirty-foot bronze legs with a wire sac cradling real marble eggs overhead: who sculpted the towering "Maman" spiders honoring her mother?
ahaFactoid: Far from horror, Bourgeois called spiders clever, protective healers—honoring her weaver mother who spent her days patiently mending antique cloth!

stem: Studio Easel Klaxon! Three of these fine-art material rules are pure paint-box science, while one wet-medium claim dries completely wrong. Catch the myth!

stem: Scribbling a red crayon heart on a torn envelope in the back of a Manhattan cab in 1977—and doing the job completely pro bono—which graphic legend designed "I ♥ NY"?

stem: Edge-to-edge electric matte ultramarine—zero brush lines, zero figures, pure buzzing cobalt velvet—whose patented 1960 pigment formula turned a single color into a trademark?

stem: Design Desk Klaxon! Three of these iconic style-history milestones check out cleanly, while one legendary German art-school timeline runs two decades too long. Nab the lie!

stem: Gallery Ledger, 1533: Stretching a ghostly skull across the carpet of Holbein's The Ambassadors, the optical trick called [ _____ ] snaps sharp only from the side.

stem: Twelve trip-wired cameras lined along a Palo Alto track in 1878 snap crisp frames of galloping mare Sallie Gardner—proving horses go airborne for which photographer?

stem: Tech Wire, May 1997: Stunned after resigning in just nineteen moves of Game 6 in Manhattan, reigning chess king Garry Kasparov lost a landmark match to IBM's [ _____ ].

stem: Rolled out on July 1, 1963 with a jaunty cartoon mailman named Mr. ZIP begging letter writers to add five digits, what stood for "Zone Improvement Plan"?

stem: Newsroom Klaxon! Three of these 20th-century tech breakthroughs hit the exact wire record, while one famous 1969 lunar broadcast memory adds extra hue. Spot the myth!
ahaFactoid: To save weight and bandwidth, Apollo 11's iconic first step beamed down on a black-and-white slow-scan TV camera—color arrived on Apollo 12!

stem: Dousing everyone from Bill Gates and Lady Gaga to Kermit the Frog during summer 2014, which viral video craze raised over $115 million for ALS research in eight weeks?
ahaFactoid: Far from a fleeting stunt, those donations directly funded scientists who discovered NEK1—a major new ALS gene—and sped up a new FDA-approved drug!

stem: California Wire, July 1955: Sinking heels into wet asphalt while counterfeit tickets doubled crowds on live ABC TV, [ _____ ] survived its chaotic "Black Sunday" debut.
ahaFactoid: During a morning plumbers' strike, Walt Disney had to pick working fountains or restrooms—wisely choosing restrooms, though guests blamed soda!

stem: Swapping a beloved 99-year-old soda formula in April 1985 sparked 400,000 angry calls, basement hoarding, and a retreat just 79 days later: what fizzled flop was it?
ahaFactoid: When skeptics whispered the fiasco was a sly marketing stunt, Coca-Cola chief Donald Keough laughed: "We're not that dumb, and we're not that smart!"

stem: A foil cylinder 335 miles above Earth whose first 1990 star snapshots came back heartbreakingly fuzzy—until spacewalking astronauts fitted optical "eyeglasses" in 1993!

stem: Nestling smooth Mexican beach pebbles inside air-holed cardboard boxes with a cheeky training manual, adman Gary Dahl sold 1.5 million of what quirky 1975 fad?
ahaFactoid: Bought at a builders' yard for a penny apiece and sold for $3.95 each, those zero-maintenance stones made Dahl an instant holiday millionaire!

stem: Paris Wire, December 2024: Five years after its blazing spire toppled before horrified TV viewers worldwide, ringing bells welcomed crowds back inside restored [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Hewing 2,000 French oaks with medieval hand axes, 2,000 craftspeople also scrubbed centuries of soot off the limestone to reveal dazzling cream walls!

stem: In October 1969, UCLA student Charley Kline tried typing "LOGIN" to Stanford 350 miles away—crashing after just "LO" during the debut of which proto-Internet network?
ahaFactoid: Professor Leonard Kleinrock beamed that no scripted line could top accidental "LO"—echoing Samuel Morse's famed 1844 message, "Lo and behold!"

stem: Candy-striped hollow Marlex plastic rings spinning furiously around millions of suburban 1958 waists—selling 25 million in four months for Wham-O: name this instant craze!
ahaFactoid: Inspired by Australian kids twirling bamboo rings, Wham-O couldn't patent a plain circle—so cheap knockoffs ended the craze almost as fast as it rose!

stem: Signed into law in January 1974 to stretch rationed gasoline during the OPEC embargo—and protested later by rocker Sammy Hagar—what became the U.S. speed limit?
ahaFactoid: To dodge drivers cranking past the cap, U.S. automakers temporarily marked 55 mph in bold red numerals on speedometers and capped dials at 85 mph!

ahaFactoid: Because Nobel Prizes are never awarded posthumously, Franklin had passed away four years before Watson, Crick, and Wilkins won the 1962 prize!

stem: Signing off every CBS show with "Good night, and good luck" after covering London's Blitz live, which news titan confronted Senator Joseph McCarthy on See It Now?
ahaFactoid: Murrow and producer Fred Friendly let McCarthy sink himself by airing the senator's own blistering quotes—drawing 15-to-1 letters cheering Murrow!

stem: Beamed coast-to-coast by NBC on New Year's Day 1954—when barely a few thousand color sets existed—which Pasadena floral spectacle marked nationwide color TV's debut?
ahaFactoid: RCA stationed prototype $1,000 color sets inside downtown hotel lobbies and shop windows across 21 cities so crowds could press noses to the glass!

stem: Press Wire, June 1971: Secretly copying 7,000 classified Vietnam pages at night, analyst Daniel Ellsberg sparked the historic [ _____ ] Supreme Court press-freedom clash.
ahaFactoid: When courts paused the New York Times, the Washington Post grabbed the baton—winning a landmark 6-to-3 Supreme Court victory against censorship!

stem: A sleek white submarine dangling a round steel sphere under gasoline tanks dives seven miles down in January 1960: where did bathyscaphe Trieste touch bottom?

stem: Halting Denver runways while choppers chased a drifting silver Mylar saucer for two tense hours in October 2009, which viral hoax ended when a kid crawled from his attic?

stem: Warning of a haunting future morning with zero birdsong from unchecked DDT spraying, which 1962 Rachel Carson bestseller launched the modern environmental movement?

stem: Directed by Ridley Scott and aired once during Super Bowl XVIII, an athletic sledgehammer-thrower smashed Big Brother's giant screen to unveil which personal computer?

stem: Arkansas Wire, September 1957: Escorted up Central High's steps by the 101st Airborne under President Eisenhower's orders, brave Black teens entered history as the [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Nine months later, senior Ernest Green became Central High's first Black graduate—with Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. sitting proudly in the family section!

stem: A sleek white dart-winged airliner cruising at Mach 2 whose pointed nose hydraulically tilts downward for landing so pilots can actually spot the runway: name this 1976 icon!

stem: Teletype Klaxon! Three of these headline dates match the front-page archive, while one infamous Washington hotel break-in timeline drops two years too late. Spot the myth!

stem: Strolling to the Paris 2024 Olympic shooting line in regular glasses, zero blinder lenses, and one hand casually tucked in his pocket to win silver, who went viral?

stem: Space Wire, July 1976: Snapped over the Cydonia plain by NASA's Viking 1 orbiter, low midday sunlight cast eerie shadows across a mile-wide mesa dubbed the [ _____ ].
ahaFactoid: Tabloids hailed an ancient alien monument for twenty years—until sharp 1998 Mars Global Surveyor photos revealed an ordinary wind-eroded flat-topped hill!

stem: Gathering 730 delegates from 44 Allied nations at a grand New Hampshire mountain resort in July 1944, which summit birthed the World Bank, IMF, and gold-pegged dollar order?

stem: Painted VW microbuses, beaded necklaces, and 100,000 flower-crowned wanderers packing Victorian porches near Golden Gate Park in 1967: name this San Francisco intersection!
ahaFactoid: By October 1967, overwhelmed locals staged a mock funeral—"The Death of Hippie"—parading a cardboard coffin stuffed with beads and tour-bus flyers!

stem: After seven Chicago deaths from laced capsules in 1982, Johnson & Johnson pulled 31 million bottles and invented triple tamper-evident seals to rescue which brand?
ahaFactoid: That swift $100 million recall remains the business-school gold standard of crisis ethics—and gave every medicine bottle on Earth foil neck seals!
